input.rationale: The verification finding says the count draws on sources outside the voter set the target describes, and the honest thing to settle before the budget closes is how far that exposure reaches. Reading the consumers answers it: a verify future is constructed only in the public VerifyLeader, every other reference either registers it on the leader or answers it with not-leader in the follower and candidate loops, and no other in-tree path creates one. So the exposure is confined to that one API and to callers that use it as a read guard; it does not touch commitment, elections or the lease, which each compute over voters. I am narrowing the saved behaviour's conditions on its existing id rather than adding a new entry, because the mechanism is unchanged and only its reach is now stated: the earlier conditions named the topologies in which the mismatch can be reached and left the producer set open, and they now name the single producer as well. Nothing else is added and no execution is spent.

knowledge.statement: verifyLeader credits the leader with one vote before consulting any configuration and sets the target to quorumSize, which counts voters only, then registers the verification future on every entry of the leader's replication state; that state holds one entry per member of the latest configuration other than the local node, non-voting members included, because startStopReplication creates entries for all of them. Each heartbeat acknowledgement runs notifyAll, which calls vote on every registered future, and vote increments the count towards the target without checking the acknowledging member's suffrage. The count therefore draws on sources that may hold no vote twice over - the leader's own unconditional credit and the acknowledgements of non-voting members - and the exposure is confined to this one API, because a verify future is constructed only in the public VerifyLeader and no other in-tree path creates one.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any leader whose latest configuration contains non-voting members, or whose latest configuration no longer includes the local node as a voter - the window after a leader has appended its own removal or demotion and before that entry commits - whenever the public VerifyLeader is called or an application uses that verification to guard a read. The producer set is closed: VerifyLeader is the only constructor of a verify future in the package, so commitment, elections and the lease check are outside this exposure, each of them computing over voters.
knowledge.changed_premise: The premise is narrowed in its reach rather than changed in direction: the earlier statement named the two sources of votes that fall outside the voter set the target is computed over and the topologies in which they can be reached, and reading the consumers shows the producer set is a single public entry point, VerifyLeader, with every other reference either registering the future on the leader or answering it in the follower and candidate loops. The mechanism is unchanged; what is added is that the exposure cannot arise through any other in-tree path, which is the boundary a reader needs in order to judge the finding's scope.

knowledge.statement: Raft.GetConfiguration() returns a configurationsFuture whose configurations field carries only latest (the atomic latestConfiguration copy), and ConfigurationFuture.Index() returns configurations.latestIndex, so the value a caller receives from Index() is 0 on every call regardless of the cluster's committed or latest configuration index. The authoritative index r.configurations.latestIndex lives only on the main thread and reaches callers solely through the configurationsCh request path (raft.go:882-890, snapshot.go:155).
knowledge.conditions: Any Raft instance, running or started with skipStartup (including the package-level GetConfiguration helper, api.go:445-458 which the doc claims has identical behavior); GetConfiguration is documented as returning the latest configuration, which may be uncommitted.

knowledge.statement: Raft.Stats() sets latest_configuration_index from the future returned by GetConfiguration(), so the published value is the constant string "0" even on a bootstrapped cluster whose configuration entry sits at index >= 1, while the same future supplies a non-empty latest_configuration. A Stats() consumer therefore cannot distinguish clusters by configuration index, and the key is constant rather than observed.
knowledge.conditions: Any node that serves Stats() while its GetConfiguration branch runs; applies to leader and follower alike.

knowledge.statement: nextConfiguration applies the caller's precondition only when change.prevIndex > 0; AddVoter/AddNonvoter/RemoveServer/DemoteVoter pass the caller-supplied prevIndex through unchanged, so passing 0 (the value the public API returns for the configuration index) silently converts a conditional configuration change into an unconditional one.
knowledge.conditions: The leader-loop configuration change path of this revision; requires the caller to have obtained prevIndex from the public API.

knowledge.statement: On one running bootstrapped three-node cluster (term 2, commit_index 3, applied_index 3), the elected leader's main thread held configuration index 1 (latest and committed, 3 voter servers), while the same instance's public GetConfiguration().Index() was 0 with Configuration() returning the same 3 voter servers, and Stats()["latest_configuration_index"] was "0" next to a non-empty latest_configuration. The value handed to API callers is therefore not the node's configuration index.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028, sampled while exactly one node was in Leader state, MakeCluster(3) bootstrap in one process with one committed client command.

knowledge.assertion: GetConfiguration() carries only the Configuration, so Index() is 0 on every call while the main thread holds the real latest index
Stats() publishes latest_configuration_index from the same future, i.e. the constant "0"

knowledge.statement: Apply/ApplyLog and Barrier use the caller's timeout only in the select that enqueues the logFuture into applyCh; the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh (only internal restore and snapshot futures set one, raft.go:1169, raft.go:1914, snapshot.go:152), so once the send succeeds the caller's Error() waits on the internal error channel alone and neither the timeout nor Shutdown() bounds completion.
knowledge.conditions: Any caller that keeps the future returned by Apply/ApplyLog/Barrier; the window requires acceptance to succeed, which BatchApplyCh (config.go:169-174) permits without a consumer, and its documentation already states that it breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply.

knowledge.statement: Shutdown() closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown but does not drain or respond to futures already queued in applyCh; the main loop leaves its select on shutdownCh and run() returns, and runLeader's defer responds only futures already recorded on leaderState.inflight, so a duty that reached the buffer but was never dispatched has no remaining producer to complete it.
knowledge.conditions: Applies whenever a logFuture was accepted into applyCh while the main loop was occupied elsewhere and the node is then shut down; the repository's own test file already notes stuck Barrier/VerifyLeader/GetConfiguration futures after shutdown at raft_test.go:40-42.

knowledge.statement: On one real bootstrapped three-node cluster with BatchApplyCh enabled, a Barrier future handed to the caller by the public API while the leader was occupied inside its own Restore handler was never responded after Shutdown(): the node moved from state Leader at acceptance to state Shutdown, the duty remained queued in applyCh (queued_in_apply_ch=1, capacity 64) and the future's Error() had not returned after the bounded 3000 ms observation. The control Barrier on the undisturbed leader returned no error, and the occupied handler resumed afterwards (restore returned 'failed to write snapshot: unexpected EOF').
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(3) with conf.BatchApplyCh=true; the main loop occupied by a public Restore whose caller-supplied reader stalls on its first Read at the moment the Barrier is accepted; Shutdown() called after acceptance and before any consumer drains applyCh.

knowledge.assertion: Apply/ApplyLog/Barrier use the timeout only for the enqueue and the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh, so acceptance is not followed by any timeout- or shutdown-bounded completion

Shutdown() closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown without draining applyCh, and runLeader's defer responds only futures already on leaderState.inflight, so a duty left in the buffer has no remaining producer

knowledge.statement: In two independent executions on real four-node clusters whose named transfer target held no vote (target_suffrage=Nonvoter in both), LeadershipTransferToServer returned a future reporting no error while the named target never reached Leader in the observation window and ended in state Follower, the maximum cluster term advanced from 2 to 4 in both runs, and the only server observed leading was the original leader, which was in Leader state at the end of both runs. The requested transfer of authority to the named server did not take effect and was not reported as a failure, and the outcome reproduced across separate clusters and schedules.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(4) with the target demoted by a committed DemoteVoter in the same run, in each of two runs of the same fixed harness; target chosen from nodes in Follower state and still replicated to by the leader; observation window 3 s sampled every 20 ms.

history.statement: On one real four-node cluster whose named transfer target held no vote (target_suffrage=Nonvoter), LeadershipTransferToServer returned a future reporting no error, the named target never reached Leader in the 3 s observation window and ended in state Follower, the maximum cluster term advanced from 2 to 4, and the only server observed leading was the original leader, which was in Leader state at the end. The requested transfer of authority to the named server therefore did not take effect and was not reported as a failure.
history.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(4) with the target demoted by a committed DemoteVoter in the same run; target chosen from nodes in Follower state and still replicated to by the leader; Observation window 3 s, sampled every 20 ms.
history.correction: The premise changes from a single observation on one cluster to a reproduced behaviour across two independent executions: the same target suffrage, the same outcome (target never leads), the same empty transfer error and the same two-step term cost recurred, so the statement no longer rests on one run. The conditions now name both receipts and the fact that the two runs share the fixed harness and inputs, which is schedule variation rather than a broader sample. The saved uses that relied on the single-run premise are the transfer investigation 721c1688d0604614841236bb40a995b2-question-1 and the two interpretations that reasoned from that case, e847bfa0cb1b455db00f2364d7eb1610-interpretation-0 and b1ef67e81473491cb1f7a33a992bc8dd-interpretation-0; both remain valid under the stronger, reproduced premise.

knowledge.statement: On one real four-node cluster where the named transfer target held its vote (target_suffrage=Voter), LeadershipTransferToServer moved leadership to that named server: the target was the only server observed in Leader state, it was in Leader state at the end, the original leader ended in Follower state without leading again, and the maximum term advanced by one, from 2 to 3. The caller's future reported no error, the same empty value reported for the vote-less target in the paired case.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(4) with no configuration change before the transfer; target chosen from nodes in Follower state; observation window 3 s, sampled every 20 ms; separate execution from the vote-less case, same harness shape and cluster shape.

knowledge.statement: nextConfiguration's AddVoter case constructs the new server entry with Suffrage Voter and either replaces an existing member entry or appends it, so a member added through the public AddVoter API becomes a voter in the very configuration entry that adds it; no Staging state is written on that path, and Staging is only left by the Promote case, while configuration.go's own command table states that AddStaging was actually AddVoter and is deprecated in favour of it. The api.go doc comment for AddVoter still describes the opposite sequence (added as a staging server, promoted by the leader once ready), and membership.md lists catching new servers up before granting them a vote as a main goal.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any leader that processes an AddVoter configuration change request; state reached through the public API only, since Promote is not issued anywhere in the non-test code.

knowledge.statement: On one real cluster a fresh, empty node joined through the public AddVoter call became a voting member in the entry that added it: the leader's latest configuration and the new node's own latest configuration both reported suffrage Voter with three voters in the configuration, and after one original voter was disconnected a command applied subsequently still committed, which requires the newly added member's acknowledgement because only two voters remained reachable out of the three needed for a majority of three.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(2) merged with a MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1) node and fully connected, join through the public AddVoter API with protocol version 3; one original voter disconnected through the test facility before the apply; apply waited on under a bounded interval.

knowledge.assertion: the AddVoter path writes Suffrage Voter into the very entry that adds the member, so no Staging state is entered and the promotion duty the doc describes is owed by nobody

knowledge.statement: On one real cluster built the same way as the AddVoter witness but joined with the public AddNonvoter call, the new member was a Nonvoter in the leader's latest configuration with only two voters present, and after one original voter was disconnected the next applied command did not commit: the future returned leadership lost after about 50 ms and the leader ended in Follower state, while the new node still advanced its log to index 4. The same harness with AddVoter instead had commitments succeed after the identical disconnect.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(2) merged with a MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1) node, fully connected; join via public AddNonvoter at protocol version 3; one original voter disconnected through the test facility before the apply; apply waited on under a bounded interval.

knowledge.statement: Whether a command can commit after one member of a three-member configuration becomes unreachable depends on the suffrage the join call wrote: a member added with AddVoter is counted in the leader's quorum arithmetic from the entry that adds it, so a majority of two remains reachable and the command commits, while a member added with AddNonvoter is not counted, no majority remains, and the leader steps down without committing.
knowledge.conditions: Three-member configuration reached by joining a fresh node to a two-voter cluster through the public API, then disconnecting one of the two original voters; observed in this revision with the in-memory transport and the test facility's Disconnect.

knowledge.statement: The network transport classifies an AppendEntries request as a heartbeat only when the term is set, a leader address is present, the previous log entry and term are zero, there are no entries and the leader commit index is zero, and it then dispatches that request synchronously to the installed handler on the connection goroutine before waiting for the response. The installed handler is Raft.processHeartbeat, which calls appendEntries; both are documented as main-thread-only, and appendEntries runs its term logic before anything about entries matters, so an empty heartbeat with a term above the node's current term calls setState(Follower) and setCurrentTerm from that goroutine. The in-memory transport's SetHeartbeatHandler is a no-op, so this path exists only for transports that implement it.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any node whose transport implements the heartbeat fast path (for example NetworkTransport) and that has been configured through NewRaft, which installs processHeartbeat as the handler; empty heartbeats from a peer with a higher term are enough to take it.

knowledge.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance in Leader state at term 2, with its main loop provably blocked inside a handler, one empty heartbeat carrying term 3 was dispatched through a transport that installs the handler the way the network transport does and returned success, and the node's term already read 3 and its state already read Follower at the moment of sampling inside that window; both values were unchanged after the handler was released. The term adoption and the leader-to-follower transition therefore happened on the calling goroutine, not on the node's main loop.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; single-voter node bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster and started with NewRaft over an in-memory transport wrapped by a local transport that fast-paths strictly empty AppendEntries requests; main loop occupied by a public Restore whose caller-supplied reader blocks on its first Read; term and state read through the package's atomic getters.

knowledge.statement: processHeartbeat begins by checking the node's shutdown channel and returning immediately when it is closed, before it inspects the command and before appendEntries runs, and that branch never calls Respond. On the fast path the transport has already handed the request to the handler and is waiting on the response channel it supplied, and whether that waiter is ever released depends on the transport: the network transport's wait also selects on the transport's own shutdown channel, which its Close signals, while the in-memory transport's Close only disconnects its peers and never closes the shutdown channel it created, so with that transport nothing releases the waiter.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any transport that installs the heartbeat handler and any node whose shutdown channel is closed while the transport is still open. The release path is transport-supplied: NetworkTransport's Close signals the channel its response wait selects on, InmemTransport's Close does not signal its shutdown channel at all, and Raft.Shutdown's future closes the transport only when the caller waits on it.

history.statement: processHeartbeat begins by checking the node's shutdown channel and returning immediately when it is closed, before it inspects the command and before appendEntries runs, and that branch never calls Respond. On the fast path the transport has already handed the request to the handler and is waiting on the response channel it supplied, and its only escape is the transport's own shutdown channel, so a heartbeat accepted on that path while the node is shut down receives no response until the transport is closed.
history.conditions: This revision, any transport that installs the heartbeat handler (for example NetworkTransport) and any node whose shutdown channel is closed while its transport remains open; the ordinary Raft.Shutdown caller that waits on the returned future closes the transport and releases the waiter.
history.correction: The premise changes in one respect: the earlier statement treated the transport's shutdown channel as the waiter's escape and the closure of the transport as what releases it, without distinguishing transports. The network transport does provide that escape, but the in-memory transport's Close only disconnects and never closes its shutdown channel, so for that transport the accepted heartbeat has no release at all - the caller is not merely delayed until a close, it is never woken. The observed receipt is unaffected and still supports the finding; only the account of the escape is narrowed to the transport that implements one. The saved use that relied on the earlier phrasing is the interpretation at operation a3e037c016ac4e2f976d62b3165916ce, which stays valid because its operands are unchanged and only the release condition is corrected.

knowledge.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance over a transport that implements the heartbeat fast path, an empty heartbeat delivered while the node was live was answered successfully and moved its term from 2 to 3, while the identical delivery after Shutdown - node in state Shutdown at term 3 with its transport left open - received no response within the 2000 ms bound and left the term at 3, showing the handler returned before running the term logic.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; single-voter node bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster and started with NewRaft over an in-memory transport wrapped by a local transport that fast-paths strictly empty AppendEntries requests on the caller's goroutine and waits on the supplied response channel; Shutdown called without waiting on the returned future so the transport stays open.

knowledge.statement: The candidate path computes the next term as the current term plus one and then writes it through setCurrentTerm, which persists the value and stores it in memory, with no compare, lock or ordering guard around the read-modify-write pair; the term adoption path in appendEntries likewise reads the current term and writes a higher one. Because the heartbeat fast path runs appendEntries on the transport's goroutine, a higher term can be written from outside the main loop between the election's read and its write, and the election's lower value then overwrites it in memory and in the stable store.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any node whose transport implements the heartbeat fast path and which is simultaneously in an election on the main thread; the window is the interval between the term read and the term store in the candidate path, and a stable-store write of the current term is the durable record that makes the regression survive a restart.

knowledge.statement: In two independent executions of the same harness on real single-node Raft instances, after the node was deposed from leadership at term 2 to term 3 and its own election was held inside its term write, one empty heartbeat carrying term 13 delivered on the fast path was fully adopted - in-memory term 13 and persisted term 13 - and when the held write was released the node's term and persisted term fell to a value lower than the term it had already adopted and durably recorded (4 landed from the held write and 5 was written by the ordinary follower election that followed), after which the node again reached Leader state at that lower term. Both executions produced the same operands throughout.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; single-voter node bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster and started with NewRaft over an in-memory transport wrapped by a local transport that fast-paths strictly empty AppendEntries requests, with an instrumented stable store that holds the next write of the current term open once it is armed; the depose is a real empty heartbeat with a higher term so the following election is timer-driven; two runs of the same fixed harness.

history.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance, after the node was deposed from leadership at term 2 to term 3 and its own election was held inside its term write, one empty heartbeat carrying term 13 delivered on the fast path was fully adopted (in-memory term 13 and persisted term 13); when the held write was released the node's term and persisted term both became 5, lower than the term it had already adopted and durably recorded, and the node then reached Leader state at that lower term.
history.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; single-voter node bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster and started with NewRaft over an in-memory transport wrapped by a local transport that fast-paths strictly empty AppendEntries requests, with an instrumented stable store that holds the next write of the current term open once it is armed; depose done by a real empty heartbeat with a higher term so the following election is timer-driven.
history.correction: The premise changes from a single observation to a reproduced behaviour: the same harness on a fresh cluster and schedule produced the same operands at every step, so the statement no longer rests on one run. It also gains a mechanism detail the first run could not settle - the held write lands while the heartbeat has already made the node a follower, so the candidate loop never runs and the later value 5 comes from the ordinary follower election that reads the regressed term - which explains both the endpoint and why the two runs agree. The saved use that relied on the single-run premise is the interpretation at operation 192609798d744832b3cfd702dfd1c5bd, which stays valid under the stronger, reproduced premise.

knowledge.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance with the same instrumented store used by the term-regression witness, the election's term write was held open with the term and the persisted term both reading 3, and when it was released without any heartbeat being delivered the term and the persisted term became 4 and the node reached Leader state - a monotone step, with no fall below the held term.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; identical setup to the witness harness (in-memory transport wrapped for the heartbeat fast path, instrumented stable store, single-voter bootstrap, a real empty heartbeat to depose the node) with the only difference that nothing is delivered during the hold.

knowledge.statement: LogCache.GetLog validates a ring slot by comparing the cached entry's index with the requested one and otherwise falls through to the store, DeleteRange clears the whole ring before the store deletes, and StoreLogs caches exactly the pointers it was given; the in-memory store keeps the same pointers, so for that store the cache and the store hold the same objects. Every non-test producer fills the entry (index, term, timestamp) before storing it and only reads it afterwards - the leader in dispatchLogs, the follower in appendEntries, and BootstrapCluster which writes one entry and returns.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, producers inside the package, with the in-memory store or any store that keeps the pointers it is given. The agreement claim does not extend to an external caller that mutates a Log after storing it while the store copies on write.

knowledge.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance with no instrumented store, 792 empty heartbeats were delivered on the fast path across about six seconds of alternating deposition and election starts, with a term sample taken immediately after each delivery: all 792 deliveries succeeded, no sampled term fell below the highest term already adopted, and the term ended at 2390 in memory and in the stable store with the node in Follower state. No natural fall was observed in 792 delivery opportunities under this schedule.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; single-voter node over the in-memory transport wrapped for the heartbeat fast path, plain in-memory store, deliveries in bursts of twelve every sixty milliseconds, each three terms above the node's current term, spaced about two milliseconds apart, sampled after each delivery; the schedule is bursty rather than uniformly distributed in time.

knowledge.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance over a store whose write of the current-term key sleeps 3 ms before applying, 768 fast-path deliveries all succeeded and 4605 term samples were taken among them with no sample below the highest term already adopted; the term ended at 2306 in memory and in the stable store with the node in Follower state. A uniform slow term write did not produce the regression in this schedule.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; single-voter node, in-memory transport wrapped for the heartbeat fast path, store that sleeps on the current-term write only, heartbeats delivered continuously three terms above the node's current term with six samples after each; no hold-open hook of any kind.

knowledge.statement: processRPC runs checkRPCHeader before dispatching any request from the consumer channel, and that check rejects a command that does not expose a header and a header whose protocol version is below the minimum, above the maximum, or more than one version behind the node's own. processHeartbeat does not call it: it checks only the shutdown channel and then passes an AppendEntriesRequest straight to appendEntries, and the network transport's heartbeat classification requires a term, a leader address, no previous entry, no entries and no leader commit index, but no protocol version. An empty heartbeat therefore reaches appendEntries without the gate every other RPC passes.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any node whose transport implements the heartbeat fast path, for an incoming request that satisfies the transport's heartbeat classification regardless of the protocol version it advertises.

Each heartbeat acknowledgement runs notifyAll, which calls vote on every registered future, and vote increments the count towards the target without checking the acknowledging member's suffrage. The count therefore draws on sources that may hold no vote twice over: the leader's own unconditional credit, which is granted even when the latest configuration no longer gives the local node a vote, and the acknowledgements of non-voting members.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any leader whose latest configuration contains non-voting members, or whose latest configuration no longer includes the local node as a voter - the window after a leader has appended its own removal or demotion and before that entry commits - whenever VerifyLeader is called or another caller uses the verification to guard a read.

history.statement: verifyLeader counts the leader itself as one vote and sets the target to quorumSize, which counts voters only, and then registers the verification future on every entry of the leader's replication state; that state holds one entry per member of the latest configuration other than the local node, non-voting members included, because startStopReplication creates entries for all of them. Each heartbeat acknowledgement runs notifyAll, which calls vote on every registered future, and vote increments the count towards the target without checking the acknowledging member's suffrage. Acknowledgements from non-voting members therefore count towards a leader verification.
history.conditions: This revision, any leader whose latest configuration contains non-voting members, when VerifyLeader is called or another caller uses the verification to guard a read.
history.correction: The premise extends rather than changes direction: the earlier statement named acknowledgements from non-voting members as the source of votes that do not correspond to the voter set the target describes, and reading verifyLeader again shows a second source of the same kind - the leader's own vote, credited before any configuration is consulted, so a leader that the latest configuration no longer counts as a voter still starts the count at one. Both sources are instances of the same mismatch between the set the count draws on and the set the target is computed over, which is why the entry is extended on its existing id rather than duplicated. The saved use that relied on the narrower statement is the interpretation at operation 2cfc284531344e89a4293b449089c945, which stays valid and simply covers one of the two sources in its wording.

knowledge.statement: Both the candidate path's term write and the heartbeat fast path's term write go through the same stable store for the same current-term key, so the term a node visibly holds is whichever of the two writes that store applied most recently. In a store that serialises writes, the outcome is decided by the order in which the two writes take effect, not by their arrival times or durations; the term falls only when the main loop's lower write is applied after the off-thread higher one, which requires the main loop's write to be deferred behind the fast path's - for example by contending on a lock or a write pipeline that the fast path's write reaches first.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any node in which a candidate's term write and a heartbeat's term adoption are in flight together against the same stable store; a store that keeps the two writers' application order tied to their latency rather than to contention does not produce the fall.

case future := <-r.configurationsCh:
			r.mainThreadSaturation.working()
			if r.getLeadershipTransferInProgress() {
				r.logger.Debug(ErrLeadershipTransferInProgress.Error())
				future.respond(ErrLeadershipTransferInProgress)
				continue
			}
			future.configurations = r.configurations.Clone()
			future.respond(nil)

These are the main goals:
 - Bringing things in line with the description in my PhD dissertation;
 - Catching up new servers prior to granting them a vote, as well as allowing permanent non-voting members; and
 - Eliminating the `peers.json` file, to avoid issues of consistency between that and the log/snapshot.

- *Nonvoter*: a server that receives log entries but is not considered for elections or commitment purposes.
 - *Staging*: a server that acts like a nonvoter with one exception: once a staging server receives enough log entries to catch up sufficiently to the leader's log, the leader will invoke a  membership change to change the staging server to a voter.

All changes to the configuration will be done by writing a new configuration to the log. The new configuration will be in affect as soon as it is appended to the log (not when it is committed like a normal state machine command). Note that, per my dissertation, there can be at most one uncommitted configuration at a time (the next configuration may not be created until the prior one has been committed). It's not strictly necessary to follow these same rules for the nonvoter/staging servers, but we think its best to treat all changes uniformly.

for _, server := range r.configurations.latest.Servers {
		if server.ID == r.localID {
			continue
		}

		inConfig[server.ID] = true

		s, ok := r.leaderState.replState[server.ID]
		if !ok {
			r.logger.Info("added peer, starting replication", "peer", server.ID)
			s = &followerReplication{
				peer:                server,
				commitment:          r.leaderState.commitment,
				stopCh:              make(chan uint64, 1),
				triggerCh:           make(chan struct{}, 1),
				triggerDeferErrorCh: make(chan *deferError, 1),
				currentTerm:         r.getCurrentTerm(),
				nextIndex:           lastIdx + 1,
				lastContact:         time.Now(),
				notify:              make(map[*verifyFuture]struct{}),
				notifyCh:            make(chan struct{}, 1),
				stepDown:            r.leaderState.stepDown,
			}

			r.leaderState.replState[server.ID] = s
			r.goFunc(func() { r.replicate(s) })
			asyncNotifyCh(s.triggerCh)
			r.observe(PeerObservation{Peer: server, Removed: false})

Reading the consumers answers it: a verify future is constructed only in the public VerifyLeader, and every other reference in the package either registers the future on the leader or answers it with not-leader in the follower and candidate loops, with no other in-tree path creating one. The exposure is therefore confined to that single API and to applications that use it as a read guard; commitment, elections and the leader-lease check are outside it, and each of those computes over voters, which is exactly why they are unaffected while the verification is not. I recorded that as a narrowing of the saved behaviour's conditions on its existing id with a changed premise that says plainly what moved - the mechanism is unchanged and only its reach is now stated, from topologies where it can be reached to the single producer it can arise through - and added the source range for the producer so the claim is anchored. No execution was spent on it, because it is decidable by reading and the remaining budget would not have produced a receipt I could interpret. The run's substantive record is unchanged and complete on what it established: six behaviours witnessed with receipts, including the durable term regression reproduced twice with its causal control and bounded by two uninstrumented probes whose zero results are explained by application order at the shared store key rather than by latency; the protocol-gate bypass on the heartbeat fast path; the verification count drawing on sources outside the voter set, now scoped to one API; the unanswered-heartbeat case with its transport-dependent release; the scoped log-cache negative; and the knowledge corrections that record where earlier phrasing over- or under-stated what the evidence supported.

knowledge.statement: Raft.GetConfiguration() returns a configurationsFuture whose configurations field carries only latest (the atomic latestConfiguration copy), and ConfigurationFuture.Index() returns configurations.latestIndex, so the value a caller receives from Index() is 0 on every call regardless of the cluster's committed or latest configuration index. The authoritative index r.configurations.latestIndex lives only on the main thread and reaches callers solely through the configurationsCh request path (raft.go:882-890, snapshot.go:155).
knowledge.conditions: Any Raft instance, running or started with skipStartup (including the package-level GetConfiguration helper, api.go:445-458 which the doc claims has identical behavior); GetConfiguration is documented as returning the latest configuration, which may be uncommitted.

knowledge.statement: Raft.Stats() sets latest_configuration_index from the future returned by GetConfiguration(), so the published value is the constant string "0" even on a bootstrapped cluster whose configuration entry sits at index >= 1, while the same future supplies a non-empty latest_configuration. A Stats() consumer therefore cannot distinguish clusters by configuration index, and the key is constant rather than observed.
knowledge.conditions: Any node that serves Stats() while its GetConfiguration branch runs; applies to leader and follower alike.

knowledge.statement: nextConfiguration applies the caller's precondition only when change.prevIndex > 0; AddVoter/AddNonvoter/RemoveServer/DemoteVoter pass the caller-supplied prevIndex through unchanged, so passing 0 (the value the public API returns for the configuration index) silently converts a conditional configuration change into an unconditional one.
knowledge.conditions: The leader-loop configuration change path of this revision; requires the caller to have obtained prevIndex from the public API.

knowledge.statement: On one running bootstrapped three-node cluster (term 2, commit_index 3, applied_index 3), the elected leader's main thread held configuration index 1 (latest and committed, 3 voter servers), while the same instance's public GetConfiguration().Index() was 0 with Configuration() returning the same 3 voter servers, and Stats()["latest_configuration_index"] was "0" next to a non-empty latest_configuration. The value handed to API callers is therefore not the node's configuration index.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028, sampled while exactly one node was in Leader state, MakeCluster(3) bootstrap in one process with one committed client command.

knowledge.assertion: GetConfiguration() carries only the Configuration, so Index() is 0 on every call while the main thread holds the real latest index
Stats() publishes latest_configuration_index from the same future, i.e. the constant "0"

knowledge.statement: Apply/ApplyLog and Barrier use the caller's timeout only in the select that enqueues the logFuture into applyCh; the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh (only internal restore and snapshot futures set one, raft.go:1169, raft.go:1914, snapshot.go:152), so once the send succeeds the caller's Error() waits on the internal error channel alone and neither the timeout nor Shutdown() bounds completion.
knowledge.conditions: Any caller that keeps the future returned by Apply/ApplyLog/Barrier; the window requires acceptance to succeed, which BatchApplyCh (config.go:169-174) permits without a consumer, and its documentation already states that it breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply.

knowledge.statement: Shutdown() closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown but does not drain or respond to futures already queued in applyCh; the main loop leaves its select on shutdownCh and run() returns, and runLeader's defer responds only futures already recorded on leaderState.inflight, so a duty that reached the buffer but was never dispatched has no remaining producer to complete it.
knowledge.conditions: Applies whenever a logFuture was accepted into applyCh while the main loop was occupied elsewhere and the node is then shut down; the repository's own test file already notes stuck Barrier/VerifyLeader/GetConfiguration futures after shutdown at raft_test.go:40-42.

knowledge.statement: On one real bootstrapped three-node cluster with BatchApplyCh enabled, a Barrier future handed to the caller by the public API while the leader was occupied inside its own Restore handler was never responded after Shutdown(): the node moved from state Leader at acceptance to state Shutdown, the duty remained queued in applyCh (queued_in_apply_ch=1, capacity 64) and the future's Error() had not returned after the bounded 3000 ms observation. The control Barrier on the undisturbed leader returned no error, and the occupied handler resumed afterwards (restore returned 'failed to write snapshot: unexpected EOF').
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(3) with conf.BatchApplyCh=true; the main loop occupied by a public Restore whose caller-supplied reader stalls on its first Read at the moment the Barrier is accepted; Shutdown() called after acceptance and before any consumer drains applyCh.

knowledge.assertion: Apply/ApplyLog/Barrier use the timeout only for the enqueue and the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh, so acceptance is not followed by any timeout- or shutdown-bounded completion

Shutdown() closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown without draining applyCh, and runLeader's defer responds only futures already on leaderState.inflight, so a duty left in the buffer has no remaining producer

knowledge.statement: In two independent executions on real four-node clusters whose named transfer target held no vote (target_suffrage=Nonvoter in both), LeadershipTransferToServer returned a future reporting no error while the named target never reached Leader in the observation window and ended in state Follower, the maximum cluster term advanced from 2 to 4 in both runs, and the only server observed leading was the original leader, which was in Leader state at the end of both runs. The requested transfer of authority to the named server did not take effect and was not reported as a failure, and the outcome reproduced across separate clusters and schedules.

The conditions now name both receipts and the fact that the two runs share the fixed harness and inputs, which is schedule variation rather than a broader sample. The saved uses that relied on the single-run premise are the transfer investigation 721c1688d0604614841236bb40a995b2-question-1 and the two interpretations that reasoned from that case, e847bfa0cb1b455db00f2364d7eb1610-interpretation-0 and b1ef67e81473491cb1f7a33a992bc8dd-interpretation-0; both remain valid under the stronger, reproduced premise.

knowledge.statement: On one real four-node cluster where the named transfer target held its vote (target_suffrage=Voter), LeadershipTransferToServer moved leadership to that named server: the target was the only server observed in Leader state, it was in Leader state at the end, the original leader ended in Follower state without leading again, and the maximum term advanced by one, from 2 to 3. The caller's future reported no error, the same empty value reported for the vote-less target in the paired case.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(4) with no configuration change before the transfer; target chosen from nodes in Follower state; observation window 3 s, sampled every 20 ms; separate execution from the vote-less case, same harness shape and cluster shape.

knowledge.statement: nextConfiguration's AddVoter case constructs the new server entry with Suffrage Voter and either replaces an existing member entry or appends it, so a member added through the public AddVoter API becomes a voter in the very configuration entry that adds it; no Staging state is written on that path, and Staging is only left by the Promote case, while configuration.go's own command table states that AddStaging was actually AddVoter and is deprecated in favour of it. The api.go doc comment for AddVoter still describes the opposite sequence (added as a staging server, promoted by the leader once ready), and membership.md lists catching new servers up before granting them a vote as a main goal.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any leader that processes an AddVoter configuration change request; state reached through the public API only, since Promote is not issued anywhere in the non-test code.

knowledge.statement: On one real cluster a fresh, empty node joined through the public AddVoter call became a voting member in the entry that added it: the leader's latest configuration and the new node's own latest configuration both reported suffrage Voter with three voters in the configuration, and after one original voter was disconnected a command applied subsequently still committed, which requires the newly added member's acknowledgement because only two voters remained reachable out of the three needed for a majority of three.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(2) merged with a MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1) node and fully connected, join through the public AddVoter API with protocol version 3; one original voter disconnected through the test facility before the apply; apply waited on under a bounded interval.

knowledge.assertion: the AddVoter path writes Suffrage Voter into the very entry that adds the member, so no Staging state is entered and the promotion duty the doc describes is owed by nobody

knowledge.statement: On one real cluster built the same way as the AddVoter witness but joined with the public AddNonvoter call, the new member was a Nonvoter in the leader's latest configuration with only two voters present, and after one original voter was disconnected the next applied command did not commit: the future returned leadership lost after about 50 ms and the leader ended in Follower state, while the new node still advanced its log to index 4. The same harness with AddVoter instead had commitments succeed after the identical disconnect.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; MakeCluster(2) merged with a MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1) node, fully connected; join via public AddNonvoter at protocol version 3; one original voter disconnected through the test facility before the apply; apply waited on under a bounded interval.

knowledge.statement: Whether a command can commit after one member of a three-member configuration becomes unreachable depends on the suffrage the join call wrote: a member added with AddVoter is counted in the leader's quorum arithmetic from the entry that adds it, so a majority of two remains reachable and the command commits, while a member added with AddNonvoter is not counted, no majority remains, and the leader steps down without committing.
knowledge.conditions: Three-member configuration reached by joining a fresh node to a two-voter cluster through the public API, then disconnecting one of the two original voters; observed in this revision with the in-memory transport and the test facility's Disconnect.

knowledge.statement: The network transport classifies an AppendEntries request as a heartbeat only when the term is set, a leader address is present, the previous log entry and term are zero, there are no entries and the leader commit index is zero, and it then dispatches that request synchronously to the installed handler on the connection goroutine before waiting for the response. The installed handler is Raft.processHeartbeat, which calls appendEntries; both are documented as main-thread-only, and appendEntries runs its term logic before anything about entries matters, so an empty heartbeat with a term above the node's current term calls setState(Follower) and setCurrentTerm from that goroutine. The in-memory transport's SetHeartbeatHandler is a no-op, so this path exists only for transports that implement it.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any node whose transport implements the heartbeat fast path (for example NetworkTransport) and that has been configured through NewRaft, which installs processHeartbeat as the handler; empty heartbeats from a peer with a higher term are enough to take it.

knowledge.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance in Leader state at term 2, with its main loop provably blocked inside a handler, one empty heartbeat carrying term 3 was dispatched through a transport that installs the handler the way the network transport does and returned success, and the node's term already read 3 and its state already read Follower at the moment of sampling inside that window; both values were unchanged after the handler was released. The term adoption and the leader-to-follower transition therefore happened on the calling goroutine, not on the node's main loop.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; single-voter node bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster and started with NewRaft over an in-memory transport wrapped by a local transport that fast-paths strictly empty AppendEntries requests; main loop occupied by a public Restore whose caller-supplied reader blocks on its first Read; term and state read through the package's atomic getters.

knowledge.statement: processHeartbeat begins by checking the node's shutdown channel and returning immediately when it is closed, before it inspects the command and before appendEntries runs, and that branch never calls Respond. On the fast path the transport has already handed the request to the handler and is waiting on the response channel it supplied, and whether that waiter is ever released depends on the transport: the network transport's wait also selects on the transport's own shutdown channel, which its Close signals, while the in-memory transport's Close only disconnects its peers and never closes the shutdown channel it created, so with that transport nothing releases the waiter.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any transport that installs the heartbeat handler and any node whose shutdown channel is closed while the transport is still open. The release path is transport-supplied: NetworkTransport's Close signals the channel its response wait selects on, InmemTransport's Close does not signal its shutdown channel at all, and Raft.Shutdown's future closes the transport only when the caller waits on it.

history.statement: processHeartbeat begins by checking the node's shutdown channel and returning immediately when it is closed, before it inspects the command and before appendEntries runs, and that branch never calls Respond. On the fast path the transport has already handed the request to the handler and is waiting on the response channel it supplied, and its only escape is the transport's own shutdown channel, so a heartbeat accepted on that path while the node is shut down receives no response until the transport is closed.
history.conditions: This revision, any transport that installs the heartbeat handler (for example NetworkTransport) and any node whose shutdown channel is closed while its transport remains open; the ordinary Raft.Shutdown caller that waits on the returned future closes the transport and releases the waiter.
history.correction: The premise changes in one respect: the earlier statement treated the transport's shutdown channel as the waiter's escape and the closure of the transport as what releases it, without distinguishing transports. The network transport does provide that escape, but the in-memory transport's Close only disconnects and never closes its shutdown channel, so for that transport the accepted heartbeat has no release at all - the caller is not merely delayed until a close, it is never woken. The observed receipt is unaffected and still supports the finding; only the account of the escape is narrowed to the transport that implements one. The saved use that relied on the earlier phrasing is the interpretation at operation a3e037c016ac4e2f976d62b3165916ce, which stays valid because its operands are unchanged and only the release condition is corrected.

knowledge.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance over a transport that implements the heartbeat fast path, an empty heartbeat delivered while the node was live was answered successfully and moved its term from 2 to 3, while the identical delivery after Shutdown - node in state Shutdown at term 3 with its transport left open - received no response within the 2000 ms bound and left the term at 3, showing the handler returned before running the term logic.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; single-voter node bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster and started with NewRaft over an in-memory transport wrapped by a local transport that fast-paths strictly empty AppendEntries requests on the caller's goroutine and waits on the supplied response channel; Shutdown called without waiting on the returned future so the transport stays open.

knowledge.statement: The candidate path computes the next term as the current term plus one and then writes it through setCurrentTerm, which persists the value and stores it in memory, with no compare, lock or ordering guard around the read-modify-write pair; the term adoption path in appendEntries likewise reads the current term and writes a higher one. Because the heartbeat fast path runs appendEntries on the transport's goroutine, a higher term can be written from outside the main loop between the election's read and its write, and the election's lower value then overwrites it in memory and in the stable store.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any node whose transport implements the heartbeat fast path and which is simultaneously in an election on the main thread; the window is the interval between the term read and the term store in the candidate path, and a stable-store write of the current term is the durable record that makes the regression survive a restart.

knowledge.statement: In two independent executions of the same harness on real single-node Raft instances, after the node was deposed from leadership at term 2 to term 3 and its own election was held inside its term write, one empty heartbeat carrying term 13 delivered on the fast path was fully adopted - in-memory term 13 and persisted term 13 - and when the held write was released the node's term and persisted term fell to a value lower than the term it had already adopted and durably recorded (4 landed from the held write and 5 was written by the ordinary follower election that followed), after which the node again reached Leader state at that lower term. Both executions produced the same operands throughout.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; single-voter node bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster and started with NewRaft over an in-memory transport wrapped by a local transport that fast-paths strictly empty AppendEntries requests, with an instrumented stable store that holds the next write of the current term open once it is armed; the depose is a real empty heartbeat with a higher term so the following election is timer-driven; two runs of the same fixed harness.

history.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance, after the node was deposed from leadership at term 2 to term 3 and its own election was held inside its term write, one empty heartbeat carrying term 13 delivered on the fast path was fully adopted (in-memory term 13 and persisted term 13); when the held write was released the node's term and persisted term both became 5, lower than the term it had already adopted and durably recorded, and the node then reached Leader state at that lower term.
history.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; single-voter node bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster and started with NewRaft over an in-memory transport wrapped by a local transport that fast-paths strictly empty AppendEntries requests, with an instrumented stable store that holds the next write of the current term open once it is armed; depose done by a real empty heartbeat with a higher term so the following election is timer-driven.
history.correction: The premise changes from a single observation to a reproduced behaviour: the same harness on a fresh cluster and schedule produced the same operands at every step, so the statement no longer rests on one run. It also gains a mechanism detail the first run could not settle - the held write lands while the heartbeat has already made the node a follower, so the candidate loop never runs and the later value 5 comes from the ordinary follower election that reads the regressed term - which explains both the endpoint and why the two runs agree. The saved use that relied on the single-run premise is the interpretation at operation 192609798d744832b3cfd702dfd1c5bd, which stays valid under the stronger, reproduced premise.

knowledge.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance with the same instrumented store used by the term-regression witness, the election's term write was held open with the term and the persisted term both reading 3, and when it was released without any heartbeat being delivered the term and the persisted term became 4 and the node reached Leader state - a monotone step, with no fall below the held term.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; identical setup to the witness harness (in-memory transport wrapped for the heartbeat fast path, instrumented stable store, single-voter bootstrap, a real empty heartbeat to depose the node) with the only difference that nothing is delivered during the hold.

knowledge.statement: LogCache.GetLog validates a ring slot by comparing the cached entry's index with the requested one and otherwise falls through to the store, DeleteRange clears the whole ring before the store deletes, and StoreLogs caches exactly the pointers it was given; the in-memory store keeps the same pointers, so for that store the cache and the store hold the same objects. Every non-test producer fills the entry (index, term, timestamp) before storing it and only reads it afterwards - the leader in dispatchLogs, the follower in appendEntries, and BootstrapCluster which writes one entry and returns.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, producers inside the package, with the in-memory store or any store that keeps the pointers it is given. The agreement claim does not extend to an external caller that mutates a Log after storing it while the store copies on write.

knowledge.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance with no instrumented store, 792 empty heartbeats were delivered on the fast path across about six seconds of alternating deposition and election starts, with a term sample taken immediately after each delivery: all 792 deliveries succeeded, no sampled term fell below the highest term already adopted, and the term ended at 2390 in memory and in the stable store with the node in Follower state. No natural fall was observed in 792 delivery opportunities under this schedule.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; single-voter node over the in-memory transport wrapped for the heartbeat fast path, plain in-memory store, deliveries in bursts of twelve every sixty milliseconds, each three terms above the node's current term, spaced about two milliseconds apart, sampled after each delivery; the schedule is bursty rather than uniformly distributed in time.

knowledge.statement: On one real single-node Raft instance over a store whose write of the current-term key sleeps 3 ms before applying, 768 fast-path deliveries all succeeded and 4605 term samples were taken among them with no sample below the highest term already adopted; the term ended at 2306 in memory and in the stable store with the node in Follower state. A uniform slow term write did not produce the regression in this schedule.
knowledge.conditions: Captured snapshot 09193ea9b7ee4df99810e6eee7058028; single-voter node, in-memory transport wrapped for the heartbeat fast path, store that sleeps on the current-term write only, heartbeats delivered continuously three terms above the node's current term with six samples after each; no hold-open hook of any kind.

knowledge.statement: processRPC runs checkRPCHeader before dispatching any request from the consumer channel, and that check rejects a command that does not expose a header and a header whose protocol version is below the minimum, above the maximum, or more than one version behind the node's own. processHeartbeat does not call it: it checks only the shutdown channel and then passes an AppendEntriesRequest straight to appendEntries, and the network transport's heartbeat classification requires a term, a leader address, no previous entry, no entries and no leader commit index, but no protocol version. An empty heartbeat therefore reaches appendEntries without the gate every other RPC passes.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any node whose transport implements the heartbeat fast path, for an incoming request that satisfies the transport's heartbeat classification regardless of the protocol version it advertises.

knowledge.statement: verifyLeader credits the leader with one vote before consulting any configuration and sets the target to quorumSize, which counts voters only, then registers the verification future on every entry of the leader's replication state; that state holds one entry per member of the latest configuration other than the local node, non-voting members included, because startStopReplication creates entries for all of them. Each heartbeat acknowledgement runs notifyAll, which calls vote on every registered future, and vote increments the count towards the target without checking the acknowledging member's suffrage. The count therefore draws on sources that may hold no vote twice over - the leader's own unconditional credit and the acknowledgements of non-voting members - and the exposure is confined to this one API, because a verify future is constructed only in the public VerifyLeader and no other in-tree path creates one.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any leader whose latest configuration contains non-voting members, or whose latest configuration no longer includes the local node as a voter - the window after a leader has appended its own removal or demotion and before that entry commits - whenever the public VerifyLeader is called or an application uses that verification to guard a read. The producer set is closed: VerifyLeader is the only constructor of a verify future in the package, so commitment, elections and the lease check are outside this exposure, each of them computing over voters.

history.statement: verifyLeader counts the leader itself as one vote and sets the target to quorumSize, which counts voters only, and then registers the verification future on every entry of the leader's replication state; that state holds one entry per member of the latest configuration other than the local node, non-voting members included, because startStopReplication creates entries for all of them. Each heartbeat acknowledgement runs notifyAll, which calls vote on every registered future, and vote increments the count towards the target without checking the acknowledging member's suffrage. Acknowledgements from non-voting members therefore count towards a leader verification.
history.conditions: This revision, any leader whose latest configuration contains non-voting members, when VerifyLeader is called or another caller uses the verification to guard a read.
history.correction: The premise extends rather than changes direction: the earlier statement named acknowledgements from non-voting members as the source of votes that do not correspond to the voter set the target describes, and reading verifyLeader again shows a second source of the same kind - the leader's own vote, credited before any configuration is consulted, so a leader that the latest configuration no longer counts as a voter still starts the count at one. Both sources are instances of the same mismatch between the set the count draws on and the set the target is computed over, which is why the entry is extended on its existing id rather than duplicated. The saved use that relied on the narrower statement is the interpretation at operation 2cfc284531344e89a4293b449089c945, which stays valid and simply covers one of the two sources in its wording.

history.statement: verifyLeader credits the leader with one vote before consulting any configuration and sets the target to quorumSize, which counts voters only, then registers the verification future on every entry of the leader's replication state; that state holds one entry per member of the latest configuration other than the local node, non-voting members included, because startStopReplication creates entries for all of them. Each heartbeat acknowledgement runs notifyAll, which calls vote on every registered future, and vote increments the count towards the target without checking the acknowledging member's suffrage. The count therefore draws on sources that may hold no vote twice over: the leader's own unconditional credit, which is granted even when the latest configuration no longer gives the local node a vote, and the acknowledgements of non-voting members.
history.conditions: This revision, any leader whose latest configuration contains non-voting members, or whose latest configuration no longer includes the local node as a voter - the window after a leader has appended its own removal or demotion and before that entry commits - whenever VerifyLeader is called or another caller uses the verification to guard a read.
history.correction: The premise is narrowed in its reach rather than changed in direction: the earlier statement named the two sources of votes that fall outside the voter set the target is computed over and the topologies in which they can be reached, and reading the consumers shows the producer set is a single public entry point, VerifyLeader, with every other reference either registering the future on the leader or answering it in the follower and candidate loops. The mechanism is unchanged; what is added is that the exposure cannot arise through any other in-tree path, which is the boundary a reader needs in order to judge the finding's scope.

knowledge.statement: Both the candidate path's term write and the heartbeat fast path's term write go through the same stable store for the same current-term key, so the term a node visibly holds is whichever of the two writes that store applied most recently. In a store that serialises writes, the outcome is decided by the order in which the two writes take effect, not by their arrival times or durations; the term falls only when the main loop's lower write is applied after the off-thread higher one, which requires the main loop's write to be deferred behind the fast path's - for example by contending on a lock or a write pipeline that the fast path's write reaches first.
knowledge.conditions: This revision, any node in which a candidate's term write and a heartbeat's term adoption are in flight together against the same stable store; a store that keeps the two writers' application order tied to their latency rather than to contention does not produce the fall.

case future := <-r.configurationsCh:
			r.mainThreadSaturation.working()
			if r.getLeadershipTransferInProgress() {
				r.logger.Debug(ErrLeadershipTransferInProgress.Error())
				future.respond(ErrLeadershipTransferInProgress)
				continue
			}
			future.configurations = r.configurations.Clone()
			future.respond(nil)

These are the main goals:
 - Bringing things in line with the description in my PhD dissertation;
 - Catching up new servers prior to granting them a vote, as well as allowing permanent non-voting members; and
 - Eliminating the `peers.json` file, to avoid issues of consistency between that and the log/snapshot.

- *Nonvoter*: a server that receives log entries but is not considered for elections or commitment purposes.
 - *Staging*: a server that acts like a nonvoter with one exception: once a staging server receives enough log entries to catch up sufficiently to the leader's log, the leader will invoke a  membership change to change the staging server to a voter.

All changes to the configuration will be done by writing a new configuration to the log. The new configuration will be in affect as soon as it is appended to the log (not when it is committed like a normal state machine command). Note that, per my dissertation, there can be at most one uncommitted configuration at a time (the next configuration may not be created until the prior one has been committed). It's not strictly necessary to follow these same rules for the nonvoter/staging servers, but we think its best to treat all changes uniformly.

for _, server := range r.configurations.latest.Servers {
		if server.ID == r.localID {
			continue
		}

		inConfig[server.ID] = true

		s, ok := r.leaderState.replState[server.ID]
		if !ok {
			r.logger.Info("added peer, starting replication", "peer", server.ID)
			s = &followerReplication{
				peer:                server,
				commitment:          r.leaderState.commitment,
				stopCh:              make(chan uint64, 1),
				triggerCh:           make(chan struct{}, 1),
				triggerDeferErrorCh: make(chan *deferError, 1),
				currentTerm:         r.getCurrentTerm(),
				nextIndex:           lastIdx + 1,
				lastContact:         time.Now(),
				notify:              make(map[*verifyFuture]struct{}),
				notifyCh:            make(chan struct{}, 1),
				stepDown:            r.leaderState.stepDown,
			}

			r.leaderState.replState[server.ID] = s
			r.goFunc(func() { r.replicate(s) })
			asyncNotifyCh(s.triggerCh)
			r.observe(PeerObservation{Peer: server, Removed: false})
